claim: A population of perivascular cells became readily visible during the first hours after HMw dextran injection in the upper dermis of the mouse ear under steady-state conditions.
source: Remarkably, a population of perivascular cells became readily visible during the first hours after HMw dextran injection, suggesting that these mostly sessile cells were constantly taking up intravascular dextran (Figure 1A and Video 1).
evidence: Supported by intravital imaging data shown in Figure 1A and Video 1, demonstrating the visualization of perivascular cells after dextran injection.

claim: The perivascular cells that became visible after dextran injection were mostly sessile and constantly taking up intravascular dextran.
source: Remarkably, a population of perivascular cells became readily visible during the first hours after HMw dextran injection, suggesting that these mostly sessile cells were constantly taking up intravascular dextran (Figure 1A and Video 1).
evidence: Inference based on the observation that cells became visible after dextran injection and remained in place, supported by imaging data.

claim: Perivascular cells uptake two differently labeled HMw dextrans injected with a lapse of 24 hr.
source: This observation was further confirmed by monitoring the uptake of two differently labeled HMw dextrans injected with a lapse of 24 hr (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data from dextran pulse-chase assay shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Dextran+ protrusions project into the vessel lumen as non-stained regions in the vivotag channel.
source: Dextran administration followed by the subsequent injection of a non-phagocytosable tracer (vivotag) revealed the presence of dextran+ protrusions as non-stained regions in the vivotag channel projecting into the vessel lumen (Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by imaging data in Figure 1B showing dextran+ protrusions as voids in the vivotag channel.

claim: The protrusions were flapping inside the vessels, presumably deflected by the vascular flow, and even contacting circulating cells.
source: The protrusions were flapping inside the vessels, presumably deflected by the vascular flow, and even contacting circulating cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B and Videos 2–4).
evidence: Supported by video microscopy data (Videos 2-4) and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B showing dynamic behavior of protrusions.

claim: 96.67% ± 1.02% of all TRITC-dextran+ cells were CD45+ in 12-week-old animals.
source: Flow cytometry analysis of skin single-cell suspensions from 12-week-old animals showed that the 96.67% ± 1.02% of all TRITC-dextran+ cells were CD45+ and the 90.41% ± 2.06% of CD45+ TRITC-dextran+ cells corresponded to macrophages (CD64+).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data from skin single-cell suspensions.

claim: 90.41% ± 2.06% of CD45+ TRITC-dextran+ cells corresponded to macrophages (CD64+) in 12-week-old animals.
source: Flow cytometry analysis of skin single-cell suspensions from 12-week-old animals showed that the 96.67% ± 1.02% of all TRITC-dextran+ cells were CD45+ and the 90.41% ± 2.06% of CD45+ TRITC-dextran+ cells corresponded to macrophages (CD64+).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data from skin single-cell suspensions.

claim: TRITC-dextran+ macrophages represented 41.28% ± 5.66% of total skin macrophages in 12-week-old animals.
source: In addition, TRITC-dextran+ macrophages represented 41.28% ± 5.66% of total skin macrophages.
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry quantification of macrophage subsets.

claim: The TRITC-dextran+ perivascular cells are mostly macrophages identified as CD45+ F4/80high CD11c- CD11b+ or CD45+ F4/80high CD11c- CD64+ cells by FACS.
source: The phenotypic characterization of the TRITC-dextran+ perivascular cells identified them mostly as macrophages (i.e., they were either CD45+ F4/80high CD11c- CD11b+ or CD45+ F4/80high CD11c- CD64+ cells by FACS [Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1C] and CD68+ cells by whole-mount immunofluorescence staining [Figure 1—figure supplement 1D]).
evidence: Supported by FACS analysis (Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1C) and immunofluorescence staining (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).

claim: The TRITC-dextran+ perivascular cells are CD68+ cells by whole-mount immunofluorescence staining.
source: The phenotypic characterization of the TRITC-dextran+ perivascular cells identified them mostly as macrophages (i.e., they were either CD45+ F4/80high CD11c- CD11b+ or CD45+ F4/80high CD11c- CD64+ cells by FACS [Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1C] and CD68+ cells by whole-mount immunofluorescence staining [Figure 1—figure supplement 1D]).
evidence: Supported by whole-mount immunofluorescence staining data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Skin macrophages are preferentially localized around dermal blood microvessels rather than lymphatics.
source: Next, we performed a mesoscopic analysis of murine ears to characterize the spatial distribution of skin macrophages. This analysis revealed their preferential localization around dermal blood microvessels rather than lymphatics (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and Video 5).
evidence: Supported by mesoscopic analysis data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and Video 5.

claim: TRITC-dextran+ macrophages were mostly apposed to capillaries and venules.
source: Interestingly, TRITC-dextran+ macrophages were mostly apposed to capillaries and venules, possibly because the dense smooth muscle layer wrapping arterioles prevented the access of macrophages to the arteriolar lumen (data not shown).
evidence: Supported by observational data from microscopy analysis.

claim: The dense smooth muscle layer wrapping arterioles possibly prevented the access of macrophages to the arteriolar lumen.
source: Interestingly, TRITC-dextran+ macrophages were mostly apposed to capillaries and venules, possibly because the dense smooth muscle layer wrapping arterioles prevented the access of macrophages to the arteriolar lumen (data not shown).
evidence: Speculative reasoning based on anatomical observations.

claim: Endothelial cells did not detectably capture dextran under the experimental conditions.
source: Moreover, endothelial cells did not detectably capture dextran under our experimental conditions, ruling out the possibility of the endothelium making accessible the intravascular dextran to the perivascular macrophages by transcytosis (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by FACS analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B demonstrating lack of dextran uptake by CD31+ endothelial cells.

claim: The endothelium does not make intravascular dextran accessible to perivascular macrophages by transcytosis.
source: Moreover, endothelial cells did not detectably capture dextran under our experimental conditions, ruling out the possibility of the endothelium making accessible the intravascular dextran to the perivascular macrophages by transcytosis (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Inference based on the absence of dextran uptake by endothelial cells.

claim: Dextran+ macrophages embrace vessels from outside the pericyte sheath.
source: We detected dextran+ macrophages embracing vessels from outside the pericyte sheath (visualized as GFP+ cells around vessels using a nestin-eGFP reporter mouse), whereas their protrusions extended across the basement membrane (stained with anti-collagen IV) and between pericytes to reach the endothelial wall (whole-mount immunofluorescence stainings in Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by whole-mount immunofluorescence staining data shown in Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Macrophage protrusions extend across the basement membrane and between pericytes to reach the endothelial wall.
source: We detected dextran+ macrophages embracing vessels from outside the pericyte sheath (visualized as GFP+ cells around vessels using a nestin-eGFP reporter mouse), whereas their protrusions extended across the basement membrane (stained with anti-collagen IV) and between pericytes to reach the endothelial wall (whole-mount immunofluorescence stainings in Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence imaging showing spatial relationships between macrophages, basement membrane, pericytes, and endothelium.

claim: Dextran+ macrophage protrusions are aligned with endothelial junctions in vivo.
source: We also visualized dextran+ macrophage protrusions aligned with endothelial junctions in vivo by intravital microscopy by injecting i.v. an anti-CD31 antibody to stain the luminal surface of dermal microvasculature (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D and Video 6).
evidence: Supported by intravital microscopy data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D and Video 6.

claim: Macrophages insert their protrusions in the intravascular space through endothelial intercellular junctions.
source: Further analysis using orthogonal sectioning of whole-mount immunofluorescence stainings indicated that the macrophages insert their protrusions in the intravascular space through endothelial intercellular junctions (Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by orthogonal sectioning analysis shown in Figure 2B.

claim: TRITC-dextran uptake was minimal in VE-cadherin-α-catenin knock-in mice.
source: Interestingly, TRITC-dextran uptake was minimal in VE-cadherin-α-catenin knock-in mice (Figure 2C).
evidence: Supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 2C comparing dextran uptake in wild-type versus VE-cadherin-α-catenin mice.

claim: In VE-cadherin-α-catenin knock-in mice, endothelial adherens junctions are stabilized.
source: In these animals, endothelial adherens junctions are stabilized (Schulte et al., 2011), which prevents paravascular permeability and leukocyte paracellular but not transcellular diapedesis.
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work (Schulte et al., 2011) characterizing this mouse model.

claim: Stabilized endothelial adherens junctions prevent paravascular permeability and leukocyte paracellular but not transcellular diapedesis.
source: In these animals, endothelial adherens junctions are stabilized (Schulte et al., 2011), which prevents paravascular permeability and leukocyte paracellular but not transcellular diapedesis.
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work (Schulte et al., 2011) and established knowledge about junction function.

claim: The ability of dermal macrophages to access the intraluminal space is restricted in VE-cadherin-α-catenin knock-in mice.
source: The ability of dermal macrophages to access the intraluminal space is restricted in these animals, supporting the observation that macrophages can reach the vascular lumen crossing the endothelial junctions and excluding the possibility that their protrusions reach the vessel lumen via a transcellular route through endothelial cells.
evidence: Inference based on the reduced dextran uptake in VE-cadherin-α-catenin mice where junctions are stabilized.

claim: Macrophages can reach the vascular lumen by crossing the endothelial junctions.
source: The ability of dermal macrophages to access the intraluminal space is restricted in these animals, supporting the observation that macrophages can reach the vascular lumen crossing the endothelial junctions and excluding the possibility that their protrusions reach the vessel lumen via a transcellular route through endothelial cells.
evidence: Inference based on the genetic model where stabilized junctions restrict macrophage access.

claim: Macrophage protrusions do not reach the vessel lumen via a transcellular route through endothelial cells.
source: The ability of dermal macrophages to access the intraluminal space is restricted in these animals, supporting the observation that macrophages can reach the vascular lumen crossing the endothelial junctions and excluding the possibility that their protrusions reach the vessel lumen via a transcellular route through endothelial cells.
evidence: Inference based on the VE-cadherin-α-catenin model which prevents paracellular but not transcellular passage, yet restricts macrophage access.

claim: The capture of dextran by skin myeloid cells is mediated by the mannose receptor (CD206).
source: Finally, since the capture of dextran by skin myeloid cells is mediated by the mannose receptor (CD206) (Wollenberg et al., 2002), we could selectively stain the intraluminal protrusions of these dermal perivascular macrophages in vivo by injecting i.v. anti-CD206 and quantified the amount of endothelial-protruding macrophages by FACS (Figure 2D).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work (Wollenberg et al., 2002) and experimental data in Figure 2D.

claim: Intraluminal protrusions of dermal perivascular macrophages can be selectively stained in vivo by injecting i.v. anti-CD206.
source: Finally, since the capture of dextran by skin myeloid cells is mediated by the mannose receptor (CD206) (Wollenberg et al., 2002), we could selectively stain the intraluminal protrusions of these dermal perivascular macrophages in vivo by injecting i.v. anti-CD206 and quantified the amount of endothelial-protruding macrophages by FACS (Figure 2D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D demonstrating in vivo staining of macrophages with anti-CD206.

claim: There exist hitherto unidentified dermal perivascular macrophages able to protrude across endothelial junctions to reach the vascular lumen in homeostatic conditions.
source: Altogether these data indicate the existence of hitherto unidentified dermal perivascular macrophages able to protrude across endothelial junctions to reach the vascular lumen in homeostatic conditions.
evidence: Inference based on the collective experimental evidence presented in the preceding sections.

claim: Dextran+ dermal macrophages did not express GFP in chimeric animals generated by reconstituting lethally irradiated C57BL/6 mice with β-actin-GFP+ hematopoietic progenitors.
source: Unexpectedly, dextran+ dermal macrophages did not express GFP in these chimeras (Figure 3A and Video 7), indicating that they were not replaced by BM-derived macrophages after irradiation and suggesting that they could be a specialized radio-resistant subset of skin-resident macrophages never characterized before.
evidence: Supported by imaging and flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3A and Video 7.

claim: Dextran+ dermal macrophages were not replaced by BM-derived macrophages after irradiation.
source: Unexpectedly, dextran+ dermal macrophages did not express GFP in these chimeras (Figure 3A and Video 7), indicating that they were not replaced by BM-derived macrophages after irradiation and suggesting that they could be a specialized radio-resistant subset of skin-resident macrophages never characterized before.
evidence: Inference based on the absence of GFP expression in dextran+ macrophages in chimeric mice.

claim: Dextran+ dermal macrophages could be a specialized radio-resistant subset of skin-resident macrophages never characterized before.
source: Unexpectedly, dextran+ dermal macrophages did not express GFP in these chimeras (Figure 3A and Video 7), indicating that they were not replaced by BM-derived macrophages after irradiation and suggesting that they could be a specialized radio-resistant subset of skin-resident macrophages never characterized before.
evidence: Inference based on the radio-resistance demonstrated by lack of replacement after irradiation.

claim: Perivascular macrophages able to phagocytose intravascular HMw dextran were present 7d after lethal γ-irradiation without BM reconstitution.
source: In fact, we monitored the presence of perivascular macrophages able to phagocytose intravascular HMw dextran 7d after lethal γ-irradiation without BM reconstitution (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by imaging data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Reconstitution of the hematopoietic system in blood and lymphoid organs was complete after 12 weeks in chimeric mice, with a negligible residual contribution of host cells to the myeloid compartment.
source: Reconstitution of the hematopoietic system in blood and lymphoid organs was complete after 12 weeks, with a negligible residual contribution of host cells to the myeloid compartment.
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry analysis of chimerism in blood and lymphoid organs.

claim: The chimerism rate in the skin myeloid subsets exhibited a higher contribution of the host populations compared to blood and lymphoid organs, which could not be ascribed to blood reconstitution.
source: In contrast, the chimerism rate in the skin myeloid subsets exhibited a higher contribution of the host populations, which could not be ascribed to blood reconstitution (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C–D).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C–D comparing chimerism in different organs.

claim: The host radio-resistant CD45.2+ macrophages efficiently captured HMw dextran under steady-state conditions.
source: The host radio-resistant CD45.2+ macrophages efficiently captured HMw dextran under steady-state conditions and were found mostly positioned around microvessels (Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry and imaging data shown in Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Host radio-resistant CD45.2+ macrophages were found mostly positioned around microvessels.
source: The host radio-resistant CD45.2+ macrophages efficiently captured HMw dextran under steady-state conditions and were found mostly positioned around microvessels (Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: Supported by imaging data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Only host macrophages captured intraluminal dextran in parabiotic mice maintained for 6 months with a shared circulation.
source: To validate this observation in a homeostatic context devoid of irradiation, the uptake of intravascular dextran was also analyzed in parabiotic mice maintained for 6 months with a shared circulation. The results obtained were similar to those of chimeric animals, inasmuch as only host macrophages captured intraluminal dextran (Figure 3C).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data from parabiotic mice shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The existence of radio-resistant dendritic cells in the skin has been previously reported.
source: The existence of radio-resistant dendritic cells in the skin has been previously reported (Bogunovic et al., 2006; Merad et al., 2002), whereas the presence of radio-resistant dermal macrophages has remained elusive hitherto.
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work (Bogunovic et al., 2006; Merad et al., 2002).

claim: The presence of radio-resistant dermal macrophages has remained elusive prior to this study.
source: The existence of radio-resistant dendritic cells in the skin has been previously reported (Bogunovic et al., 2006; Merad et al., 2002), whereas the presence of radio-resistant dermal macrophages has remained elusive hitherto.
evidence: Statement of novelty based on lack of prior reports in the literature.

claim: STREAMs are a radio-resistant subset that coexists in steady state with other skin macrophages of radio-sensitive nature.
source: This study reveals that STREAMs are a radio-resistant subset that coexists in steady state with other skin macrophages of radio-sensitive nature.
evidence: Summary statement based on the collective experimental evidence from chimerism and parabiosis experiments.

claim: The radio-resistant macrophages described in Haniffa et al., 2009 might be the human homolog of the mouse STREAM subset.
source: In this regard, the radio-resistant macrophages described in (Haniffa et al., 2009) might be the human homolog of this mouse subset, extending the generality and impact of our findings.
evidence: Speculative inference based on similarities between the mouse subset described here and human macrophages described in cited work.

claim: STREAMs are maintained locally in the skin throughout adult life independently of circulatory precursors.
source: The chimerism, parabiosis and fate mapping experiments also indicate that STREAMs are maintained locally in the skin throughout adult life independently of circulatory precursors, as opposed to radio-sensitive macrophages that are renewed at a low rate from blood in steady state and replaced by donor BM progenitors after a genotoxic insult.
evidence: Inference based on chimerism, parabiosis, and fate mapping experimental data.

claim: Radio-sensitive macrophages are renewed at a low rate from blood in steady state and replaced by donor BM progenitors after a genotoxic insult.
source: The chimerism, parabiosis and fate mapping experiments also indicate that STREAMs are maintained locally in the skin throughout adult life independently of circulatory precursors, as opposed to radio-sensitive macrophages that are renewed at a low rate from blood in steady state and replaced by donor BM progenitors after a genotoxic insult.
evidence: Inference based on chimerism experiments showing replacement of radio-sensitive macrophages by donor cells.

claim: The data extend previous knowledge on the minimal blood exchange experienced by tissue-resident macrophages in other tissues.
source: Thus, our data further extent the previous knowledge on the minimal blood exchange experienced by tissue-resident macrophages in other tissues (Hashimoto et al., 2013; Yona et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work (Hashimoto et al., 2013; Yona et al., 2013) and the current findings.

claim: UV irradiation had a clearly negative effect on the survival and renewal of host compared with donor macrophages.
source: Chimeric CD45.1/CD45.2 (donor/host) animals were exposed to UVA-B irradiation (5 J/cm2), and ear skin was analysed after one month. UV irradiation had a clearly negative effect on the survival and renewal of host compared with donor macrophages (Figure 5A), indicating that radio-resistant macrophages are UV-sensitive.
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 5A comparing host and donor macrophages after UV irradiation.

claim: Radio-resistant macrophages are UV-sensitive.
source: UV irradiation had a clearly negative effect on the survival and renewal of host compared with donor macrophages (Figure 5A), indicating that radio-resistant macrophages are UV-sensitive.
evidence: Inference based on the differential effect of UV irradiation on host versus donor macrophages.

claim: Radio-resistant macrophages did not express langerin and are clearly distinguishable from epidermal and dermal langerin+ dendritic cells.
source: However, the radio-resistant macrophages did not express langerin and are clearly distinguishable from epidermal and dermal langerin+ dendritic cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by imaging data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A demonstrating lack of langerin expression.

claim: Host radio-resistant macrophages lack self-renewal capacity in steady-state.
source: We first treated chimeric animals intradermally with clodronate liposomes to deplete skin macrophages. Monitoring at 24 hr after injection showed depletion of both macrophage subsets, whereas after 7d we observed selective partial recovery of host macrophages, consistent with an in situ renewal of these cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 1). Then, we performed Ki-67 staining in the skin of host and donor macrophages from chimeric animals using LC as control cells endowed with self-renewal potential (Chorro et al., 2009) (Figure 5B). The results point out to host macrophages as the only cell type assayed unable to proliferate by itself in steady-state.
evidence: Supported by Ki-67 staining data shown in Figure 5B demonstrating lack of proliferation in host macrophages.

claim: Host radio-resistant macrophages have a slower turnover compared to BM-derived donor macrophages and Langerhans cells.
source: We complemented the study analysing the incorporation of BrdU administered ad libitum during 8d in these subsets (Figure 5C). The results indicate that host radio-resistant macrophages have a slower turnover compared to BM-derived donor macrophages and LC.
evidence: Supported by BrdU incorporation data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Skin radio-resistant macrophages are a long-lived differentiated population that originates from an in situ proliferating progenitor.
source: Altogether these findings suggest that skin radio-resistant macrophages are a long-lived differentiated population that originates from an in situ proliferating progenitor.
evidence: Inference based on the lack of self-renewal, slow turnover, and recovery after depletion.

claim: The relative content of resident macrophages from donor and host changed dynamically over time in favor of the dominant BM-derived pool.
source: Interestingly, the relative content of resident macrophages from donor and host changed dynamically over time in favor of the dominant BM-derived pool, which exhibits higher proliferative capacity (Figure 5D).
evidence: Supported by longitudinal flow cytometry data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Skin-resident macrophages possess no pluripotent potential per se in steady-state.
source: First, we performed an analysis of the expression of a panel of stemness-related genes demonstrating that skin-resident macrophages possess no pluripotent potential per se in steady-state (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: Supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2A.

claim: YFP+ CD45+ F4/80high CD11b+ CD11c- macrophages were detected in the homeostatic skin of Bmi1 reporter animals not earlier than 5d after i.p. injection of tamoxifen.
source: However, YFP+ CD45+ F4/80high CD11b+ CD11c- macrophages were detected in the homeostatic skin of Bmi1 reporter animals not earlier than 5d after i.p. injection of tamoxifen, suggesting that they are indeed derived from a Bmi1+ progenitor (Figure 5E).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data from Bmi1 reporter mice shown in Figure 5E.

claim: YFP+ macrophages in Bmi1 reporter animals are derived from a Bmi1+ progenitor.
source: However, YFP+ CD45+ F4/80high CD11b+ CD11c- macrophages were detected in the homeostatic skin of Bmi1 reporter animals not earlier than 5d after i.p. injection of tamoxifen, suggesting that they are indeed derived from a Bmi1+ progenitor (Figure 5E).
evidence: Inference based on the timing of YFP+ macrophage appearance after tamoxifen induction in Bmi1 reporter mice.

claim: Generation of YFP+ macrophages was increased during macrophage replenishment after depletion with s.c. clodronate treatment.
source: Generation of YFP+ macrophages was increased during macrophage replenishment after depletion with s.c. clodronate treatment (Figure 5—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2D.

claim: Perivascular YFP+ cells protruding into vessels were detected in the dermis of Bmi1 reporter animals.
source: Moreover, microscopy analysis of the dermis of these reporter animals detected perivascular YFP+ cells protruding into vessels (Figure 5F).
evidence: Supported by microscopy imaging shown in Figure 5F.

claim: YFP+ dextran+ macrophages were detected in the skin of tamoxifen-treated HMw dextran-injected chimeric mice by FACS analysis.
source: YFP+ dextran+ macrophages were detected in the skin of tamoxifen-treated HMw dextran-injected chimeric mice by FACS analysis (Figure 5G–H).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 5G–H.

claim: YFP+ dextran+ macrophages exist under steady-state conditions in chimeras lacking tamoxifen-inducible hematopoietic cells of BM origin.
source: Intravital experiments confirmed the existence of YFP+ dextran+ macrophages under steady-state conditions in chimeras lacking tamoxifen-inducible hematopoietic cells of BM origin (Figure 5I).
evidence: Supported by intravital imaging data shown in Figure 5I.

claim: Radio-resistant macrophages are generated in situ from a skin pluripotent progenitor independent of BM.
source: Together these results confirm the in situ generation of radio-resistant macrophages from a skin pluripotent progenitor independent of BM.
evidence: Inference based on the collective fate mapping and chimerism experiments with Bmi1 reporter mice.

claim: Two distinct skin-resident macrophage pools coexist in homeostasis based on their differential capacity to uptake circulating macromolecules, sensitivity to γ-irradiation and progenitor source.
source: Our results strongly imply the coexistence of two distinct skin-resident macrophage pools in homeostasis based on their differential capacity to uptake circulating macromolecules, sensitivity to γ-irradiation and progenitor source.
evidence: Summary inference based on the collective experimental evidence presented.

claim: Both host and donor macrophage subsets were F4/80high, CD11b+ and expressed similar levels of Ly6C and CD115.
source: Both subsets were F4/80high, CD11b+ and expressed similar levels of other myeloid markers such as Ly6C and CD115, as well as of the prototypic macrophage markers CD68 and CD64-MertK (whose combined expression is associated with mature tissue macrophages [Gautier et al., 2012]) (Figure 6A and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 6A and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Both host and donor macrophage subsets expressed similar levels of the prototypic macrophage markers CD68 and CD64-MertK.
source: Both subsets were F4/80high, CD11b+ and expressed similar levels of other myeloid markers such as Ly6C and CD115, as well as of the prototypic macrophage markers CD68 and CD64-MertK (whose combined expression is associated with mature tissue macrophages [Gautier et al., 2012]) (Figure 6A and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data and citation to Gautier et al., 2012.

claim: The combined expression of CD64 and MertK is associated with mature tissue macrophages.
source: Both subsets were F4/80high, CD11b+ and expressed similar levels of other myeloid markers such as Ly6C and CD115, as well as of the prototypic macrophage markers CD68 and CD64-MertK (whose combined expression is associated with mature tissue macrophages [Gautier et al., 2012]) (Figure 6A and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by citation to Gautier et al., 2012.

claim: Both host and donor macrophage subsets were CD11c- and Ly6G-.
source: Moreover, both subsets were CD11c- and Ly6G- (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claim: There was no consistent or sizeable difference in the expression of Tie-2, CD40, CD70, or MHC-I between host and donor macrophages.
source: There was also no consistent or sizeable difference in the expression of the angiogenesis-related receptor Tie-2, the costimulatory molecules CD40 and CD70 or MHC-I.
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry analysis comparing marker expression.

claim: Host radio-resistant macrophages showed higher mean expression of CD86 and CD206 compared to donor macrophages.
source: However, we found a higher mean expression of the costimulatory molecule CD86 and the mannose receptor (CD206) in the host radio-resistant subset, whereas MHC-II was elevated in the donor BM-derived subset (Figure 6A).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: MHC-II was elevated in the donor BM-derived macrophage subset compared to host macrophages.
source: However, we found a higher mean expression of the costimulatory molecule CD86 and the mannose receptor (CD206) in the host radio-resistant subset, whereas MHC-II was elevated in the donor BM-derived subset (Figure 6A).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The broad range of expression of differential markers within each macrophage subset precluded their use to dissect accurately the heterogeneity found among the skin-resident macrophages.
source: Nevertheless, the broad range of expression of these differential markers within each macrophage subset precluded their use to dissect accurately the heterogeneity found among the skin-resident macrophages (example provided for MHC-II in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B demonstrating overlapping expression.

claim: Of 17,741 genes compiled, significant differences were found in 744, with 135 corresponding to protein coding sequences with similar normalized expression levels across replicates.
source: Of 17,741 genes compiled, we found significant differences in 744, 135 corresponding to protein coding sequences with similar normalized expression levels across replicates (Figure 6B–C, and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Supported by RNA-Seq data analysis shown in Figure 6B–C and Supplementary file 1.

claim: A comprehensive Gene Set Enrichment Analysis showed 36 Kegg pathways upregulated in host radio-resistant macrophages versus 149 in donor macrophages.
source: A comprehensive Gene Set Enrichment Analysis (GSEA) of all genes expressed in at least one cell type showed 36 Kegg pathways upregulated in host radio-resistant macrophages (14 of them enriched at a nominal p-value < 1%) vs. 149 in donor macrophages (26 pathways enriched at a nominal p-value < 1%).
evidence: Supported by GSEA analysis of RNA-Seq data.

claim: The GSEA analysis confirmed striking differences in metabolism between the two resident macrophage populations in homeostatic skin.
source: The GSEA analysis confirmed striking differences in metabolism between the two resident macrophage populations in homeostatic skin (Figure 6—figure supplement 2A and Supplementary file 2).
evidence: Supported by GSEA results shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2A and Supplementary file 2.

claim: Host radio-resistant macrophages displayed a metabolic gene profile based on fatty acid oxidation and oxidative phosphorylation.
source: Host radio-resistant macrophages displayed a metabolic gene profile based on fatty acid oxidation and oxidative phosphorylation, whereas donor BM-derived macrophages showed a glycolytic gene profile.
evidence: Supported by GSEA analysis of metabolic pathways.

claim: Donor BM-derived macrophages showed a glycolytic gene profile.
source: Host radio-resistant macrophages displayed a metabolic gene profile based on fatty acid oxidation and oxidative phosphorylation, whereas donor BM-derived macrophages showed a glycolytic gene profile.
evidence: Supported by GSEA analysis of metabolic pathways.

claim: Host radio-resistant macrophages have elevated mitochondrial function compared to donor macrophages.
source: Direct staining of the skin with an indicator of mitochondrial membrane potential (MitoTracker Orange CMTMRos) revealed elevated mitochondrial function in host radio-resistant macrophages, although both macrophage subsets contained comparable amounts of mitochondria per cell (as indicated by similar levels of Tomm20, a translocase of the outer mitochondrial membrane) (Figure 6—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Both host and donor macrophage subsets contained comparable amounts of mitochondria per cell.
source: Direct staining of the skin with an indicator of mitochondrial membrane potential (MitoTracker Orange CMTMRos) revealed elevated mitochondrial function in host radio-resistant macrophages, although both macrophage subsets contained comparable amounts of mitochondria per cell (as indicated by similar levels of Tomm20, a translocase of the outer mitochondrial membrane) (Figure 6—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: Supported by Tomm20 staining data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2B.

claim: The metabolic profiles of donor and host macrophages in homeostatic skin mirrored the metabolic reprogramming of pro-inflammatory classically activated and anti-inflammatory alternatively activated macrophages.
source: Thus, the metabolic profiles of donor and host macrophages in homeostatic skin mirrored the metabolic reprogramming of pro-inflammatory classically activated and anti-inflammatory alternatively activated macrophages (Galvan-Pena and O'Neill, 2014), respectively.
evidence: Inference based on comparison with established metabolic profiles of M1 and M2 macrophages, supported by citation.

claim: Donor-derived macrophages showed increased expression of H2-Eb1, Ccr2, Il1β, Il6 and Il10.
source: Donor-derived macrophages showed increased expression of genes such as H2-Eb1 (coding for MHC-II), Ccr2, Ilβ, Il6 and Il10.
evidence: Supported by qPCR data validating RNA-Seq findings.

claim: Il1β, Il6 and Il10 code for cytokines related to the pro-inflammatory response in macrophages.

evidence: Supported by multiplex cytokine analysis data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: The anti-inflammatory macrophage subset did not produce significant amounts of pro-inflammatory cytokines and chemokines in response to LPS.
source: Interestingly, the pro-inflammatory macrophages became activated and produced substantial levels of CCL4, CCL5, CXCL1, TNF-α and IL-6 (among other pro-inflammatory mediators examined) in comparison to control conditions, whereas the anti-inflammatory subset did not produce significant amounts of these cytokines and chemokines in response to LPS (Figure 7D).

claim: The anti-inflammatory macrophages produced IL-10 in response to IL-4 stimulation.
source: However, the anti-inflammatory macrophages produced IL-10 in response to IL-4 stimulation (Figure 7E).

source: These results suggest that the anti-inflammatory macrophages have a dearth of functional plasticity, being refractory to pro-inflammatory challenges but responsive to anti-inflammatory stimuli.

claim: The different subsets of skin-resident macrophages could be already committed even since steady-state to perform non-redundant functions.

claim: OVA fluospheres injected i.v. were specifically captured by skin macrophages.

claim: The capture of OVA fluospheres by skin macrophages was abrogated after depletion of skin macrophages by s.c. clodronate treatment.

claim: The macrophages able to capture OVA fluospheres were dextran+ in C57BL/6 wt animals.

evidence: Supported by intravital imaging and flow cytometry data shown in Figure 8C, Figure 8—figure supplement 1A, and Videos 8–9.

claim: The macrophages able to capture OVA fluospheres were radio-resistant in CD45.1/CD45.2 (donor/host) C57BL/6 chimeras.

evidence: Supported by flow cytometry and imaging data shown in Figure 8D–E.

claim: The amount of OVA-coated beads captured by skin STREAMs was low compared with that of splenic macrophages.
source: The availability of blood-borne nanoparticles in peripheral circulation is limited by the filtering action of mainly the liver and spleen, and therefore the amount of OVA-coated beads captured by skin STREAMs was low compared with that of splenic macrophages (Figure 8—figure supplement 1B); however, this amount was increased in γ-irradiated and splenectomized animals (Figure 8—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The amount of OVA-coated beads captured by skin STREAMs was increased in γ-irradiated and splenectomized animals.
source: The availability of blood-borne nanoparticles in peripheral circulation is limited by the filtering action of mainly the liver and spleen, and therefore the amount of OVA-coated beads captured by skin STREAMs was low compared with that of splenic macrophages (Figure 8—figure supplement 1B); however, this amount was increased in γ-irradiated and splenectomized animals (Figure 8—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1A.

claim: DT-OVA-NP treatment depleted preferentially STREAMs while preserving most of the other skin macrophages.
source: Based on the specific ability of STREAMs to capture OVA nanoparticles, we next set up a method to deplete them selectively by administering i.v. OVA-coated nanoparticles (NP) adsorbed with diphtheria toxin (DT). In contrast to the i.v. administration of clodronate liposomes, which failed to eradicate skin STREAMs (data not shown), this tailored experimental strategy depleted preferentially STREAMs preserving most of the other skin macrophages that had no access to the blood-borne toxin-coated NPs (Figure 9—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 9—figure supplement 1.

claim: Macrophage depletion with DT-OVA-NP was associated with a significant delay in the healing process at mid-stage of repair.
source: Animals were treated either with OVA-NP or DT-OVA-NP (2.5 μl/g per dose) 1d before and 2d after wounding and were sacrificed at d5, observing a clear decrease in the macrophage population (Figure 9A,D). At this mid-stage of repair, macrophage depletion was associated with a significant delay in the healing process (measured as % of area of initial wound) (Figure 9B) and the histological analyses revealed a marked reduction in the formation of granulation tissue, concomitant reduced angiogenesis as well as delayed re-epithelialization (Figure 9C–D).
evidence: Supported by wound area measurements shown in Figure 9B.

claim: Macrophage depletion with DT-OVA-NP resulted in a marked reduction in the formation of granulation tissue, concomitant reduced angiogenesis and delayed re-epithelialization.
source: At this mid-stage of repair, macrophage depletion was associated with a significant delay in the healing process (measured as % of area of initial wound) (Figure 9B) and the histological analyses revealed a marked reduction in the formation of granulation tissue, concomitant reduced angiogenesis as well as delayed re-epithelialization (Figure 9C–D).
evidence: Supported by histological analysis shown in Figure 9C–D.

claim: Administration of DT-OVA-NP 2d after wounding resulted in a clear defect in collagen deposition.
source: Next, we administered a sole dose (2.5 μl/g) of DT-OVA-NP 2d after wounding and monitored wound closure till d9. In this manner, the macrophage depletion was attained after the initial inflammatory phase of wound healing (Gurtner et al., 2008). The Masson trichrome staining demonstrated a clear defect in collagen deposition in the animals treated with DT-OVA-NP (Figure 10A).
evidence: Supported by Masson trichrome staining data shown in Figure 10A.

claim: The defect in collagen deposition correlated with the disordered distribution of myofibroblasts in DT-OVA-NP treated animals.
source: This defect correlated with the disordered distribution of myofibroblasts in these animals observed with the α-smooth muscle actin (SMA) staining (Figure 10B).
evidence: Supported by α-SMA staining data shown in Figure 10B.

claim: STREAMs could exert a prominent role as the macrophages involved in orchestrating tissue remodeling and repair in skin.

evidence: Inference based on the wound healing defects observed after STREAM depletion and their anti-inflammatory profile.

claim: No substantial differences were observed in wound closure, collagen deposition, and myofibroblast distribution in Ccr2-/- mice compared to Ccr2+/+ animals.

evidence: Supported by wound healing data shown in Figure 10—figure supplement 1F–G.

claim: The results strengthen the idea of the selective role for STREAMs in tissue repair.

evidence: Inference based on the collective wound healing experiments in different genetic models.

claim: STREAMs capture blood-borne macromolecules by extending protrusions into the vascular lumen at steady-state.

evidence: Summary statement based on the collective experimental evidence.
